MultipleChoice.prompt: This function is meant to choose the question format for a whole session: Experts get open questions only when the author has enabled them, and every other case gets multiple choice. The caller passes the `open_questions` configuration flag. Which line is the bug, and why?
options: The wildcard arm should return Open so that Novices and Intermediates also get open questions when the flag is on.
The match is not exhaustive, so the code does not compile unless a separate arm is added for Level::Intermediate.
The format is computed once per level, so a session would alternate between Open and MultipleChoice from one question to the next.
The Expert arm ignores `open_questions`, so Experts get open questions even when the opt-in flag is off.
reasons: Wrong. Open questions are reserved for Experts, and every other level must get multiple choice, so this would change the policy instead of fixing the bug.
Wrong. The wildcard arm covers Novice and Intermediate, so the match is exhaustive and compiles. The problem is the unused flag, not exhaustiveness.
Wrong. The function depends only on the level and the flag, which do not change within a session, so the format is the same for every question. Alternating would need a question index as input.
Correct. Open questions must be opt-in, so the Expert arm needs a guard on the flag. Without it the flag is accepted but never used, and every Expert gets open questions regardless of configuration.

questions.explanation: Wrong. The function depends only on the level and the flag, which do not change within a session, so the format is the same for every question. Alternating would need a question index as input.

MultipleChoice.prompt: A settings file sets `open_questions = true`. The user then runs the tool with the CLI flag explicitly set to false, and the higher-priority layer should win. With the overlay shown, the final value is still true. Which replacement for the flawed line fixes this while still treating an unset CLI/env value as 'no opinion'?
reasons: `unwrap_or` returns a `bool` here, and the field is an `Option<bool>`, so this does not compile. Even if the types lined up, it would be resolving a value too early instead of overlaying.

The lower layer still takes precedence, so the CLI or env value is ignored whenever the file sets one. The extra `.or(Some(false))` also bakes the default into the overlay, when it should be applied once at the end.
This compiles, but it turns an unset higher layer into an explicit false. That wipes out a true from the file whenever the flag is not passed, which is exactly what `Option` was meant to prevent.

`over.or(self)` keeps the higher-priority value when it is set, even if it is `Some(false)`, and falls back to the lower layer only when it is `None`. So a file value of true is overridden by an explicit false on the CLI, and kept when the CLI says nothing.

MultipleChoice.prompt: Look at the snippet. What happens when it runs, and why?
options: It prints `choice`: the guard is false, so the Expert arm is skipped and the wildcard arm matches.
It fails to compile, because a guarded arm does not count towards exhaustiveness and the wildcard cannot cover Expert.
It prints `open`, because the pattern `Level::Expert` matches and the guard only filters afterwards.
It panics at runtime, because no arm matches an Expert when `open` is false.
reasons: A guarded arm matches only if its pattern matches and its guard is true. With `open` false the guard fails, so matching goes on to the next arm. The wildcard catches that Expert value, as well as Novice.
The compiler does ignore guarded arms when checking exhaustiveness. That is exactly why the wildcard is needed, and the wildcard does cover Expert, so the code compiles.
The guard is part of the arm's condition, not a later filter. If the guard is false, the arm is not taken at all.
The wildcard arm matches every value that earlier arms did not take, so some arm always matches. Rust would reject a non-exhaustive match at compile time, not panic.

MultipleChoice.prompt: A team changes its question policy so that open questions are off by default, and only authors at the Expert level get them when the option is enabled. An existing Gherkin scenario says a known Expert author starts a session and every question is open. It has no configuration step. After the change the scenario fails. What is the right way to update the acceptance spec, and why?
options: Loosen the Then step so it accepts either multiple-choice or open questions for an Expert.
Leave the scenario unchanged, because the Expert level by itself implies open questions whatever the configuration says.
Set the default configuration back to open questions on, so the existing Expert scenarios pass without edits.
Add a Given step that turns open questions on in the scenario's world config before the session starts. The scenario then states the non-default configuration it relies on.
reasons: This makes the scenario pass but removes its value. It would no longer check that enabling open questions changes the format for Experts, so regressions in the policy would go unnoticed.
Under the new policy the level only picks the format when open questions are enabled. With the default off, an Expert gets multiple-choice questions, so the unchanged scenario would fail.
This undoes the policy being introduced just to avoid editing specs. The acceptance specs should follow the intended default, and a separate scenario now asserts that the default is off.

The default is now off, so an Expert scenario that expects open questions depends on a non-default setting. Each scenario sets its own world config, so the precondition is visible in the spec and the scenario passes for the right reason.

questions.explanation: The default is now off, so an Expert scenario that expects open questions depends on a non-default setting. Each scenario sets its own world config, so the precondition is visible in the spec and the scenario passes for the right reason.
